# Summary

Permutation tests replace a theoretical reference distribution with one generated by rearranging the observed data. The rearrangements must be valid under the null hypothesis: unrestricted shuffling is inappropriate when observations are temporally or spatially ordered, clustered, blocked, or collected using a hierarchical experimental design. `permute` is an R package for describing such exchangeability structures and generating permutation indices from them. Its principal design vocabulary and restricted schemes were developed from those introduced by Cajo J. F. ter Braak in CANOCO 3.1 and refined in later CANOCO versions [@terBraak1990; @terBraakSmilauer2012]. `permute` makes these ideas available as reusable, model-independent R objects. Users can generate individual permutations, random sets, or complete enumerations, while package authors can accept the same design objects in different statistical procedures. The package supports free permutations, cyclic shifts for series and transects, toroidal shifts for rectangular grids, blocks, plots, and nested or split-plot designs.

# Statement of need

The validity of a permutation test rests on exchangeability under the null hypothesis. When all observations are exchangeable, a random ordering from `sample()` may suffice. Many real data sets have a more constrained structure. Repeated observations from a site cannot be exchanged freely with observations from other sites; the order of a time series or transect should be retained; a regular spatial grid may require shifts that preserve neighbourhood relationships; and whole plots and subplots may need to be permuted at different levels.

Encoding these restrictions separately in every analysis function is difficult to test and encourages subtle inconsistencies. `permute` separates the permutation design from both the data and the test statistic. A design constructed once can be inspected, checked, updated, enumerated, and passed to downstream software. This serves two audiences: analysts who need valid randomizations for non-trivial sampling designs, and package developers who need a stable interface for adding permutation inference to their own methods. The small hard-dependency footprint also makes `permute` suitable as infrastructure rather than an analysis framework that dictates a particular model.

# State of the field

CANOCO established a practical vocabulary for Monte Carlo permutation tests in ecological ordination, including unrestricted permutations, cyclic shifts for time series or linear transects, toroidal shifts for rectangular grids, blocks, and hierarchical or split-plot restrictions [@terBraak1990; @terBraak1992; @terBraakSmilauer2012]. The corresponding schemes in `permute` derive directly from this work. They include cyclic and toroidal shift procedures connected to the spatial Monte Carlo testing literature discussed by @besagClifford1989. `permute` implements the resulting finite exchangeability schemes rather than the Markov-chain Monte Carlo procedures that form the principal methodological contribution of Besag and Clifford. It deliberately carries the CANOCO design lineage into R and does not claim these schemes as inventions of the package.

R software involving permutations falls into several overlapping groups. Test-oriented packages supply inferential procedures: `coin` implements conditional inference for independence problems [@hothorn2008coin], `exactRankTests` provides exact rank and permutation tests [@exactRankTests], `flip` supplies multivariate permutation and rotation tests [@flip], `lmPerm` targets linear models [@lmPerm], and `permuco` covers regression, repeated-measures ANOVA/ANCOVA, and signal comparisons [@frossardRenaud2021]. Combinatorics packages instead generate or manipulate mathematical arrangements: `arrangements`, `RcppAlgos`, and `gtools` enumerate permutations and combinations [@arrangements; @RcppAlgos; @gtools], while `partitions` and `permutations` address integer or set partitions and algebraic permutations [@hankin2006; @hankinWest2007; @hankin2020]. `randomizeR` generates and evaluates treatment-allocation procedures for clinical trials [@uschner2018]. Domain-facing packages such as `vegan` perform analyses and consume permutation designs [@vegan].

| Category | Examples | Purpose | Restrictions and statistics |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statistical tests | `coin`, `permuco`, `flip` | Test-specific inference | Method-dependent restrictions; statistics supplied |
| Combinatorics | `arrangements`, `RcppAlgos` | Enumerate mathematical arrangements | No exchangeability design or statistic |
| Trial allocation | `randomizeR` | Generate treatment sequences | Allocation rules; assessments supplied |
| Analysis | `vegan` | Ecological analyses | Consumes `permute` designs; statistics supplied |
| Design infrastructure | `permute` | Generate admissible rearrangements | Series, grids, blocks, plots, and hierarchies; no statistic |

The distinct role of `permute` is therefore to represent admissible rearrangements independently of the statistic evaluated on them. Its fixed-size `partition` design randomizes assignment to groups while preserving their sizes; it is not an implementation of additive integer partitions, general set partitions, or symmetric-group algebra.

# Software design

A permutation design has three composable levels. Blocks are the outermost level: observations never move between blocks. Plots sit within blocks and may themselves be permuted. The within level controls rearrangement of observations inside plots, or of the whole data set when no higher levels are present. `how()` combines these components, while `Plots()` and `Within()` configure their behaviour. Grouping variables may be supplied directly or described using formulas.

For example, the following design keeps observations within sites, applies the same cyclic time shift within each site, and creates a reusable matrix of permutation indices:

```r
library("permute")

site <- gl(4, 5)
control <- how(
  plots = Plots(strata = site, type = "none"),
  within = Within(type = "series", constant = TRUE),
  nperm = 999
)
set.seed(42)
perms <- shuffleSet(length(site), control = control)
```

The available schemes reflect the CANOCO lineage: free rearrangement; cyclic series or transect shifts; toroidal grid shifts; optional mirroring; and separate restrictions at block, plot, and within-plot levels. `permute` extends and exposes these ideas through explicit R control objects, symmetric-grid constraints, and fixed-size assignment partitions. `check()` validates whether a requested design can be applied, `numPerms()` counts its possible permutations, and `allPerms()` enumerates sufficiently small sets. `shuffle()` returns one ordering and `shuffleSet()` returns a matrix whose rows can be reused across statistics or parallel workers. `permutations()` applies generated indices to a vector, while `permutator()` offers sequential access to a supplied or generated set. Stored control metadata and compatibility with R's seeded random-number generator support reproducible analyses.

# Research impact statement

`permute` originated as permutation infrastructure in `vegan` and was separated into its own package so that the same implementation could be used by other analysts and package authors. It has been developed publicly for more than fifteen years and has been distributed through CRAN since 2011. At the time of writing, 28 CRAN packages directly depend on or import `permute`, with additional packages suggesting it. These include `vegan`, `permuco`, `randomizationInference`, `indicspecies`, and `codyn`, spanning community ecology, experimental analysis, randomization inference, indicator-species analysis, and temporal diversity research.

This use reflects the value of separating design generation from model fitting. `vegan`, for example, exposes `permute` controls across permutation-based ordination and ecological testing rather than maintaining a second representation of blocks and restricted designs. Other packages can accept either a control object or a pre-generated matrix, giving users a consistent way to state the randomization design and making it easier to reproduce exactly the set of permutations used in an analysis. Extensive automated tests exercise random generation, complete enumeration, hierarchical designs, validation, and seeded behaviour across operating systems. The result is focused infrastructure: `permute` does not attempt to select a test statistic or fit an analysis model, but provides the exchangeability layer on which those procedures can rely.
